pages.title: Opening a File
bullets:
Before we can read the contents of the file, we must tell Python which file we are going to work with and what we will be doing with the file
This is done with the open() function
open() returns a “file handle” - a variable used to perform operations on the file
Similar to “File -> Open” in a Word Processor
pages.pdf_text:
Opening a File
• Before we can read the contents of the file, we must tell Python
which file we are going to work with and what we will be doing
with the file
• This is done with the open() function
• open() returns a “file handle” - a variable used to perform
operations on the file
• Similar to “File -> Open” in a Word Processor

pages.title: Using open()
bullets:
handle = open(filename, mode)
returns a handle use to manipulate the file
filename is a string
mode is optional and should be 'r' if we are planning to read the file and 'w' if we are going to write to the file
fhand = open('mbox.txt', 'r')
pages.pdf_text:

• mode is optional and should be 'r' if we are planning to

pages.title: The newline Character
bullets:
We use a special character called the “newline” to indicate when a line ends 
We represent it as \n in strings 
Newline is still one character - not two

>>> stuff = 'Hello\nWorld!'
>>> stuff
'Hello\nWorld!'
>>> print(stuff)
Hello
World!
>>> stuff = 'X\nY'
>>> print(stuff)
X
Y
>>> len(stuff)
3

pages.title: Reading Files in Python
pages.pdf_text: Reading Files in Python

pages.title: File Handle as a Sequence
bullets:
A file handle open for read can be treated as a sequence of strings where each line in the file is a string in the sequence
We can use the for statement to iterate through a sequence
Remember - a sequence is an ordered set
pages.pdf_text:
File Handle as a Sequence
• A file handle open for read can
be treated as a sequence of
strings where each line in the
file is a string in the sequence
• We can use the for statement
to iterate through a sequence
• Remember - a sequence is an
ordered set
xfile = open('mbox.txt')
for cheese in xfile:
    print(cheese)

pages.title: Counting Lines in a File
bullets:
Open a file read-only
Use a for loop to read each line
Count the lines and print out the number of lines

fhand = open('mbox.txt')
count = 0
for line in fhand:
    count = count + 1
print('Line Count:', count)


$ python open.py
Line Count: 132045

pages.title: Reading the *Whole* File
bullets: We can read the whole file (newlines and all) into a single string

>>> fhand = open('mbox-short.txt')
>>> inp = fhand.read()
>>> print(len(inp))
94626
>>> print(inp[:20])

pages.title: Searching Through a File
bullets: We can put an if statement in our for loop to only print lines that meet some criteria
pages.pdf_text:
Searching Through a File
We can put an if statement in
our for loop to only print lines
that meet some criteria
fhand = open('mbox-short.txt')
for line in fhand:
    if line.startswith('From:') :
        print(line)

bullets:
We can strip the whitespace from the right-hand side of the string using rstrip() from the string library
The newline is considered “white space” and is stripped

pages.title: Skipping with continue
bullets: We can conveniently skip a line by using the continue statement
pages.pdf_text:
Skipping with continue
We can conveniently
skip a line by using the
continue statement
fhand = open('mbox-short.txt')
for line in fhand:
    line = line.rstrip()
    if not line.startswith('From:') :
        continue
    print(line)

We can look for a string
anywhere in a line as our

pages.pdf_text:
Bad File
Names
  fname = input('Enter the file name:  ')
  try:
      fhand = open(fname)
  except:
      print('File cannot be opened:', fname)
      quit()
  count = 0
  for line in fhand:
      if line.startswith('Subject:') :
          count = count + 1
  print('There were', count, 'subject lines in', fname)
